_about: Recommended response for each attack class EVNet Sentinel detects, split by who acts. These are standard defensive measures for each attack mechanism, adapted to an OCPP/ISO 15118 charging network. They are guidance for operators; they were not themselves tested in this project. Edit freely -- the dashboard and simulation console read this file through src/evaluation/export_insights.py.

dos.label: Denial of service
dos.summary: Someone is trying to overwhelm a charging station or the management system so it stops responding.
dos.impact: Stations lose their OCPP link to the CSMS: heartbeats stop, sessions cannot be authorised or billed, and remote control (start, stop, reset, price updates) fails. Drivers see a station that will not start a charge.

owner: Confirm stations are configured for OCPP offline operation, so they keep charging and queue transactions locally while the CSMS link is down.
Check the station display and local logs: a station that has lost its CSMS link should be visibly flagged to drivers rather than failing silently.
csms: Watch for stations dropping heartbeats together; a burst of simultaneous disconnects points at the network, not at individual stations.
Enforce per-connection and per-source rate limits on the OCPP WebSocket endpoint, ideally at a reverse proxy in front of the CSMS.
Hold off remote resets of affected stations until the flood stops — a reset during an attack just adds reconnect load.
analyst: Identify the source address or addresses and block them at the edge firewall.
Enable upstream DDoS scrubbing or ISP-level filtering if the volume exceeds what the local link can absorb.
Capture a short packet sample for the incident record before blocking, so the attack can be characterised later.

recon.label: Reconnaissance
recon.summary: Someone is mapping the charging network — finding which devices exist, which ports are open, and what software they run. Nothing is broken yet, but this is usually the step before an attack.
recon.impact: No direct outage. The risk is what comes next: an attacker who knows the firmware version and open services can target a known vulnerability in the station or the CSMS.

owner: Make sure station firmware is current — reconnaissance is typically looking for a known, unpatched weakness.
Ask the vendor which ports the station needs; anything beyond OCPP to the CSMS and the local ISO 15118 link to the vehicle should be closed.
csms: Require OCPP security profile 2 or 3 (TLS, with client certificates in profile 3) so a mapped station still cannot be impersonated.
Review recent configuration changes and authorisation attempts from the stations that were scanned.
analyst: Find the scanning device. In this testbed that was either a host on the station wifi or a compromised vehicle on the charging cable — they call for different containment.
Put charging stations on an isolated network segment that only permits traffic to the CSMS.
Raise monitoring on the scanned hosts: a follow-up exploitation attempt is the thing to catch.

recon.uncertainty: The detector reliably recognises that a scan is happening but often cannot tell which nmap mode it is — they emit nearly identical traffic. Respond to it as reconnaissance; do not wait for the exact scan type.

SYN_Flood.what: Floods the target with TCP connection requests (SYN packets) that are never completed, filling the table of half-open connections so real stations cannot connect.

analyst: Enable SYN cookies on the CSMS host (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1) and shorten the SYN-RECEIVED timeout.
csms: Expect OCPP reconnect storms once the flood ends; stagger station reconnection if the platform supports it.

TCP_Flood.what: Floods the target with established-looking TCP traffic to exhaust bandwidth and connection-handling capacity.

analyst: Cap concurrent connections per source address and drop traffic from sources exceeding it.

UDP_Flood.what: Floods the target with UDP datagrams to saturate its link.

analyst: OCPP runs over TCP. Charging stations need very little UDP (DNS, NTP) — rate-limit or drop all other inbound UDP to them.

SynonymousIP_Flood.what: Floods the target with packets whose source address is forged to match the target's own address, so the victim ends up replying to itself.

analyst: Drop any inbound packet whose source address equals its destination, and apply anti-spoofing ingress filtering (BCP 38 / unicast reverse-path forwarding).

PSHACK_Flood.what: Floods the target with TCP packets carrying PUSH and ACK flags that do not belong to any real connection, forcing it to process each one.

analyst: Use a stateful firewall that drops TCP segments not belonging to a tracked connection.

ICMP_Flood.what: Floods the target with ICMP echo (ping) requests.

analyst: Rate-limit ICMP echo at the edge; charging stations do not need to answer ping from outside their segment.

ICMP_Fragmentation.what: Sends fragmented ICMP packets that force the target to spend memory and CPU reassembling them.

analyst: Drop fragmented ICMP at the edge and set conservative reassembly limits on exposed hosts.

Slowloris_Scan.what: Opens many connections to a web server and keeps each one alive by sending a request extremely slowly, until the server has no connections left for real clients. OCPP-J runs over WebSocket, which starts as an HTTP request, so the CSMS endpoint is exposed to this.

csms: Put the OCPP WebSocket endpoint behind a reverse proxy with short header and body timeouts and a per-address connection cap.
analyst: Look for many long-lived, near-idle connections from a single source — that pattern, not volume, is the signature.

TCP_Port_Scan.what: Probes a range of ports to find which ones are open.

analyst: Compare the scanned ports against what each station is supposed to expose; any unexpected open port is the finding.

SYN_Stealth_Scan.what: A port scan that sends connection requests but never completes them, to avoid appearing in application logs.

analyst: Application logs will show nothing for this one — rely on firewall and IDS logs to see its extent.

Service_Version_Detection.what: Connects to open ports and asks each service what software and version it is running.

owner: Remove version banners from station services where the vendor allows it.
analyst: Check the versions that were exposed against known vulnerabilities.

OS_Fingerprinting.what: Sends crafted packets and studies the replies to work out the target's operating system.

analyst: Knowing the OS narrows which exploits apply — confirm the station's OS is patched.

Aggressive_Scan.what: nmap's -A mode: port scan, service versions, OS detection and default scripts together. Loud, fast and thorough.

analyst: An aggressive scan returns a complete picture of the target in one pass; treat the scanned hosts as fully mapped.

Vulnerability_Scan.what: Actively tests the target for known exploitable weaknesses. This is the closest reconnaissance gets to an attack.

owner: Contact the station vendor: confirm the firmware has no known unpatched vulnerabilities.
csms: Audit the scanned stations' configuration and credentials; rotate them if there is any doubt.
analyst: Treat as an active incident. Isolate the source immediately and review the target hosts for signs of compromise.
